column5: Hebrew zkr; name in the night
column6: The commentary names ẕakara as keeping the Lord's name alive; the psalmist remembers YHWH's name in the night and keeps Torah, joining recollection to sustained practice.

column5: Hebrew zkr with shem
column6: The commentary's Arabic remembrance of the Lord's name has a close Hebrew counterpart: after revealing the name YHWH, God calls it a memorial for every generation.

column5: Hebrew zkr and honoring the name
column6: Those who fear YHWH speak together and esteem his name; he attends and a book of remembrance is written for them, joining remembered name, reverence, and a recorded outcome.

column5: Hebrew zkr; invoking the name in danger
column6: Against those relying on chariots and horses, the community remembers the name of YHWH; this makes the commentary's remembered name a ground of trust in its own crisis setting.

column5: Hebrew zkr and shem
column6: The psalm pairs YHWH's enduring name with his remembrance through generations, giving the commentary's name-and-remembrance relation a communal, lasting form.

column5: Hebrew zeker, remembrance
column6: The righteous rejoice in YHWH and give thanks to his holy remembrance; the Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ẕikr is used in praise.

column5: Hebrew zkr; remembering the name
column6: In a prayer about waiting for YHWH, the speaker says that his name and memorial are the soul's desire; remembrance is a continuing orientation, not merely spoken repetition.

column5: Name remembered at an altar
column6: At the altar God says he will come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this joins invoked name, worship place, and blessing as the commentary does in its temple reading.

column5: Remembering YHWH with prayer
column6: From the fish, Jonah remembers YHWH and says his prayer reaches the holy temple; the crisis prayer makes remembrance lead directly into bodily and verbal appeal.

column5: Wholehearted praise and the feared name
column6: The psalmist asks for an undivided heart to fear God's name; this gives a concrete inward counterpart to the commentary's account of remembrance held in heart as well as tongue.

column5: Wholehearted praise glorifies the name
column6: The speaker thanks God with the whole heart and glorifies his name forever, bringing inward recollection and voiced praise together.

column5: Blessing and lifted hands in the name
column6: After seeking God in the sanctuary, the speaker blesses him while alive and lifts his hands in his name; remembrance becomes an embodied act of praise.

column5: Bowing before the Maker
column6: The worshippers bow, kneel, and fall before the one who made them; the verse supplies a direct bodily scene for the commentary's transition from remembered name to prayer.

column5: Clean hands and a pure heart
column6: The person who approaches God's holy place has clean hands and a pure heart and does not lift the soul to falsehood; this makes the commentary's purification-before-prayer sequence concrete.

column5: A generation seeking God's face
column6: The verse names those who seek God's face as Jacob, following the clean-handed worshipper of the prior verse; purification is framed as entrance into a praying community.

column5: Calling and publicizing the name
column6: The speaker tells the people to call on YHWH's name and make his deeds known among nations; the name remembered in 87:15 becomes publicly voiced testimony.

column5: Calling on the name and recounting deeds
column6: The psalm joins thanksgiving, calling on YHWH's name, and making his deeds known; its own sequence links remembrance to public praise.

column5: The name blessed continually
column6: The servants are told to bless YHWH's name from now and forever, extending the commentary's single remembered name into enduring communal praise.

column5: Praise from sunrise to sunset
column6: YHWH's name is praised from the rising to the setting of the sun; this gives a daily rhythm to the commentary's remembered name and prayer.

column5: The name placed on the people as blessing
column6: The priests place YHWH's name on Israel and God blesses them; this supplies the communal and reciprocal side of the commentary's name-and-prayer relation.

column5: The temple as the place of God's name
column6: Solomon asks that God's eyes attend the house where he said his name would dwell, and that he hear prayer directed there; the text links name, place, and prayer.

column5: Hearing prayer and forgiving
column6: Solomon asks God to hear the supplication of king and people from heaven and forgive; the temple name in the preceding verse frames the communal prayer.

column5: Abram builds an altar and calls on YHWH
column6: Abram's worship at Bethel combines an altar with calling on YHWH's name, a patriarchal instance of the prayerful life that the commentary says reaches back to Abraham.

column5: Abraham calls on the eternal God's name
column6: After planting a tamarisk at Beersheba, Abraham calls on the name of YHWH, the everlasting God; the scene joins a living planted object and invocation in Abraham's own setting.

column5: Isaac builds an altar and calls on YHWH
column6: Isaac builds an altar and invokes YHWH's name at Beersheba, showing the prayer practice associated with Abraham continuing in his son.

column5: Rabbinic derivation of daily prayer from the patriarchs
column6: The Talmud reads Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as instituting the daily prayers from their biblical encounters; it develops the commentary's Abrahamic prayer lineage into a regular liturgical schedule.

column5: Words kept on the heart
column6: Israel is told to keep the commandment's words on the heart; this matches the commentary's secondary account of ẕikr as guarding the Lord's name inwardly.

column5: Remembering through ordinary bodily routines
column6: The words are to be recited sitting, walking, lying down, and rising; this places remembrance throughout daily embodied life, as the commentary's name moves from speech into prayer.

column5: Do not forget the Lord
column6: Israel is warned not to forget the God who brought them from Egypt; the explicit negative makes the memory-versus-forgetting contrast developed around 87:15 concrete.

column5: Serving and swearing by God's name
column6: The next verse commands service of YHWH and oath by his name, so the remembered name issues in bodily allegiance rather than remaining an idea.

column5: Named people humble themselves, pray, and turn
column6: God's people called by his name are to humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from evil; the response closely joins purification, name, and prayer.

column5: The Lord proclaims his name to Moses
column6: YHWH descends and proclaims his name to Moses, making the name a revealed address before Moses responds in worship in verse 8.

column5: Moses bows after hearing the name
column6: After YHWH proclaims his name and character, Moses hastens to bow to the earth and worship; this gives the commentary's word-to-body movement a specific scene.

column5: Calling on the name while receiving salvation
column6: The worshipper lifts the cup of salvation and calls on YHWH's name; the prayerful name is set within a response to deliverance.

column5: Thanksgiving sacrifice and calling on the name
column6: The speaker offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name, joining prayer, praise, and embodied offering.

column5: Blessing the name and announcing salvation
column6: The psalm orders blessing YHWH's name and announcing his salvation day by day, a direct public form of remembering the name.

column5: The name, offering, and entry to worship
column6: Worshippers ascribe glory due God's name, bring an offering, and enter his courts; this gives the commentary's remembered name a concrete liturgical destination.

column5: Prayer as incense and hands as offering
column6: The psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and lifted hands be accepted as an evening offering; this directly joins verbal prayer to bodily worship.

column5: Entering worship with thanks and blessing the name
column6: The people enter God's gates with thanksgiving and bless his name in the courts, showing the communal form of the individual prayer in the commentary.

column5: The Lord's name alone is exalted
column6: The psalm says God's name alone is exalted above earth and heaven; this concretely meets the commentary's secondary image of the name as what rises above obscurity.

column5: One Lord and one name over the earth
column6: The prophet's final vision says YHWH will be one and his name one; this gives a textual counterpart to the commentary's claim that the worshipper remembers a name belonging to no rival.

column5: The Lord's Prayer begins by hallowing the name
column6: Jesus teaches disciples to address the Father and hallow his name before asking for daily provision; this directly joins remembered divine name and prayer.

column5: Prayer in secret before the Father
column6: Jesus contrasts the public performance of hypocrites with a disciple praying unseen, where the Father sees what is hidden; this sharpens the commentary's contrast between voiced and inward remembrance.

column5: Syriac ṣlōṯā for prayer
column6: The Peshitta uses the Syriac cognate ṣlōṯā for prayer in Jesus' warning about hypocritical synagogue and street prayer; it shows the shared Semitic prayer term in a concrete liturgical context.

column5: Wash away sins and call on the name
column6: Ananias tells Saul to be baptized, wash away sins, and call on Jesus' name; this tightly combines purification, invocation, and embodied religious action.

column5: Calling on the Lord's name and being saved
column6: Paul cites the promise that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, directly joining invocation of the name with the commentary's affirmed salvation.

column5: The name bestowed above every name
column6: God highly exalts Jesus and gives him the name above every name; this is a direct textual counterpart to the commentary's secondary image of a name being raised.

column5: Every knee bows at the name
column6: The next verse says every knee bows at Jesus' name, meeting the commentary's movement from named word to bodily prayer while retaining its different scene.

column5: Every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
column6: The following verse makes every tongue confess Jesus as Lord; voiced confession completes the name-and-body sequence in the hymn.

column5: Syriac ṣlōṯā and hallowing the Name
column6: In the Peshitta's Lord's Prayer the cognate ṣlōṯā introduces a prayer whose first petition hallows the Father's name, uniting the commentary's two key actions in one Semitic-language witness.

column5: Praise as sacrifice and confession of the name
column6: The community is urged to offer a continual sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips confessing Jesus' name; this joins verbal remembrance with worship as an enacted offering.

column5: Bodies offered as worship
column6: Paul asks believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, their rational worship; this gives a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's name moving immediately into bodily prayer.

column5: A community calling on Jesus' name
column6: Paul identifies the church with all who call on the name of Jesus as Lord; the ayah's single person's remembrance is here a shared communal practice.

column5: Naming the Lord entails turning from evil
column6: The saying joins everyone who names the Lord's name with departure from unrighteousness; it makes the commentary's purification and invocation a linked ethical identity.

column5: Cornelius prays continually and gives alms
column6: Cornelius is described as devout, God-fearing, generous to the poor, and constant in prayer; this is a specific portrait in which ethical giving and prayer mark one person.

column5: Prayers and alms as a memorial before God
column6: The angel says Cornelius' prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial before God; the scene joins prayer, ethical action, and remembrance with a reversal in which God receives the remembrance.

column5: Prostration and prayers rising as incense
column6: The elders fall before the Lamb, holding incense bowls identified as the prayers of the saints; this combines bodily bowing and prayer in one scene.

column5: Prayer as an ongoing practice
column6: Paul's short instruction to pray continually makes prayer a sustained orientation rather than an isolated utterance, matching the commentary's completed life portrait.

column5: The Shema as the first confession
column6: Jesus begins his answer with Israel's confession that the Lord is one; this provides the remembered monotheistic formula that frames the ensuing command to love and serve God.

column5: Love God with the whole person
column6: The next verse commands love with heart, soul, mind, and strength; this supplies an embodied, inward allegiance behind the commentary's prayerful remembrance.

column5: Hannah's bitter prayer and vow
column6: Hannah prays at Shiloh and vows her son to YHWH; the scene gives a particular Hebrew Bible portrait of a person defined by a prayerful response.

column5: YHWH remembers Hannah after her prayer
column6: The narrative says YHWH remembers Hannah and she conceives; unlike 87:15's person remembering God, this reverses the direction of remembrance and makes prayer's answer the point.

column5: Aramaic cognate ṣlōṯā in the house of prayer
column6: The Targum's Aramaic rendering calls the temple a house of prayer for all peoples; its ṣlōṯā cognate to Arabic ṣalāt meets the commentary's movement from a single worshipper to shared sacred spaces.

column5: Aramaic ṣlōṯā for prayer as incense
column6: The Targum uses the Aramaic prayer word cognate with ṣalāt in a verse likening prayer to incense; its context also associates raised hands with an evening offering.

column5: Priestly praise followed by the people's prostration
column6: In Simon's temple service, instruments and praise accompany the sacrifice and the assembly bows; this gives a communal liturgical scene for the commentary's bodily prayer.

column5: The first calling on YHWH's name
column6: The verse says people began to call on YHWH's name, an early counterpart to the commentary's remembered name; the wider genealogy makes this an origin of public worship.

column5: Solomon's prayer toward the house bearing God's name
column6: Solomon asks that God's eyes remain open toward the house where his name dwells and that he hear prayer; this expands the temple-name relation into a royal prayer.

column5: Hallowing the name in a repeated daily prayer
column6: The Didache transmits the Lord's Prayer with its hallowed-name petition and instructs its repeated daily recitation; it shows early Christian liturgy making the name-and-prayer connection habitual.

column5: The tax collector's humble bodily prayer
column6: The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, and asks for mercy; his prayer's posture and humility give a specific counterpoint to a merely external religious act.

column5: The humble worshipper goes home justified
column6: Jesus says the tax collector, rather than the self-exalting Pharisee, goes home justified; this connects a person's enacted humility and prayer with the commentary's portrait of the one who prospers through purification.

column5: Prayer rises with incense before God
column6: An angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the altar; this provides a heavenly liturgical image for the commentary's pairing of prayer and praise.

column5: Praise offered from within a fiery furnace
column6: Azariah opens his mouth to pray amid the furnace and bless God; the commentary explicitly treats its second, corrective fire only as a lexical echo, so this is a limited comparison where fire becomes the setting for prayer rather than its punishment.

column5: Purified lips call the name and serve
column6: YHWH says he will purify the peoples' lips so they call his name and serve him shoulder to shoulder; this tightly joins purification, voiced remembrance, and worship as in the ayah's sequence.

column5: Refining fire followed by calling the name
column6: The remnant is refined like silver and gold, then calls on YHWH's name and receives his answer; this links the commentary's purification-to-prayer chain with its expressly secondary fire image.

column5: Prayer rejected despite lifted hands
column6: YHWH refuses many prayers and hides his eyes because the worshippers' hands are full of blood; this warns that the commentary's prayerful portrait cannot be reduced to outward ritual.

column5: Wash and make yourselves clean
column6: The prophet commands washing and cleansing immediately after rejected prayer; the text makes ethical purification a necessary preparation for accepted worship.

column5: Learn good and seek justice
column6: The next verse defines cleansing through concrete justice and care for the vulnerable, supplying an ethical dimension to the commentary's person identified by deeds.

column5: Lips honor God while the heart is distant
column6: Isaiah says the people honor God with lips while their hearts are far away and their worship is learned formula; this counters a merely vocal reading of remembering the name.

column5: The whole self blesses the holy name
column6: The psalmist commands the inner self to bless YHWH and all within to bless his holy name; this directly joins the commentary's remembrance in tongue and heart.

column5: Do not forget the Lord's benefits
column6: The next verse warns the soul not to forget God's benefits; the Hebrew forget/memory contrast reinforces the commentary's account of ẕikr against oblivion.

column5: Bowing in the temple and thanking God's name
column6: The psalmist bows toward the holy temple, thanks God's name, and says God has exalted his word; this joins the commentary's name, bodily prayer, worship place, and elevation image.

column5: The great and holy name praised
column6: The nations are told to praise God's great and awesome name because it is holy; this makes the name's exalted status a liturgical confession.

column5: Bow at God's footstool
column6: The worshippers are told to exalt YHWH and bow at his footstool; the verse pairs a raised divine name with a body lowered in worship.

column5: Glory due the name and bodily worship
column6: The psalm asks worshippers to ascribe glory due YHWH's name and bow in holy splendor; it puts name-praise and bodily prostration together.

column5: The Lord's name majestic over all earth
column6: The psalm opens by calling YHWH's name majestic throughout the earth; this gives a direct scriptural counterpart to the commentary's image of the name rising above obscurity.

column5: David asks that God's name be magnified forever
column6: In David's prayer, the desired result is that YHWH's name be magnified forever; this is a direct prayer-context for the commentary's elevated-name image.

column5: The assembly blesses God's exalted name
column6: The Levites call the people to bless YHWH's glorious name, exalted above blessing and praise; a gathered community performs the name-praise that 87:15 gives one person.

column5: Proclaiming the name and ascribing greatness
column6: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God; this links the named Lord with voiced praise and elevation.

column5: Remembering God's wonders in a name-praising psalm
column6: After calling on YHWH's name and recounting his deeds, the psalm tells Israel to remember his wonders; Hebrew zkr is used for the preserving remembrance developed in the commentary.

column5: Kneeling and thanking God three times a day
column6: Daniel kneels toward Jerusalem three times daily and prays with thanks as he had done before; this is a concrete portrait of remembered allegiance enacted through the body.

column5: A plea for mercy because of God's name
column6: Daniel asks God to hear and see the city's desolation, explicitly appealing to mercy rather than human righteousness; the prayer gives a counterweight to any idea that purification earns rescue.

column5: Hear for your sake and for the city called by your name
column6: Daniel asks the Lord to hear, forgive, and act for his own sake because the city and people bear his name; it joins prayer, name, and communal identity.

column5: Foreigners pray toward the house because of God's name
column6: Solomon includes the foreigner who comes because of God's great name and prays toward the temple, asking that God hear so all peoples know the name; this expands the commentary's house-of-prayer image beyond one community.

column5: The foreigner comes because of God's name
column6: Solomon's dedication prayer explicitly imagines a foreigner coming from far away because of YHWH's name; the name draws worshippers to the house.

column5: Hearing a foreigner's prayer makes the name known
column6: Solomon asks God to hear the foreigner's prayer so all peoples may know and fear his name; prayer at the named house becomes public witness.

column5: The temple called a house of prayer for all peoples
column6: The prophet promises foreigners access to God's holy mountain and calls the house a house of prayer for all peoples; this directly grounds the commentary's move from an individual's prayer to worship spaces.

column5: The name honored among nations with incense and offering
column6: YHWH's name is great among the nations, where pure offerings and incense are presented from sunrise to sunset; the text joins name-praise, prayer-like worship, and the daily horizon.

column5: A clean heart requested from God
column6: In David's penitential prayer, he asks God to create a clean heart; purification is petitioned as a divine act before the speaker's later praise.

column5: Cleaned lips open to praise
column6: The psalmist asks God to open his lips so his mouth will declare praise; this gives a direct purification-to-verbal-worship sequence.

column5: Meditating on Torah day and night
column6: The righteous person's delight and meditation in Torah provide a specific scriptural form of continual remembrance, related to the commentary's name held alive through ordinary life.

column5: The righteous person as a fruitful tree
column6: The meditator is like a tree planted by streams, bearing fruit and prospering; this meets the commentary's explicit crop-growth image for purification without claiming a shared story or cognate.

column5: God's name and greatness have no equal
column6: Jeremiah says none is like YHWH and that his name is great in might; this concretizes the commentary's exclusive, exalted divine name.

column5: Thanksgiving and an ordered way lead to salvation
column6: God says the one offering thanksgiving honors him and the one ordering his way rightly will see salvation; this joins praise to enacted conduct rather than speech alone.

column5: The community magnifies YHWH's name together
column6: After the psalmist blesses YHWH, he invites others to magnify the Lord and exalt the name together; the individual remembrance becomes communal praise.

column5: Seeking YHWH and receiving an answer
column6: The speaker says he sought YHWH and was answered and delivered; this provides a prayer-and-response sequence alongside the commentary's person who remembers and prays.

column5: Rabbinic reading of the first invocation as profanation
column6: A remembered rabbinic interpretation of Genesis 4:26 construes the early calling on YHWH's name as profaning or redirecting it toward idols; it warns that naming God can be corrupted rather than honored, though the precise gloss wording should be checked.

column5: Abram prays to the Creator after rejecting idols
column6: After Abram rejects his father's idols, Jubilees gives him a prayer to the Creator; this expands the commentary's Abrahamic prayer lineage into an explicit repudiation of false worship.

column5: The faithful bless God's name from the furnace
column6: In the Greek addition to Daniel, the prayer in the furnace blesses the God of the ancestors and praises his name; unlike the condemned fire in the commentary's neighboring portrait, this fire becomes a setting for faithful prayer.

column5: Jesus applies Isaiah's lips-and-heart critique
column6: Jesus cites Isaiah's contrast between honoring God with lips and having a distant heart; this Christian reuse makes the commentary's inward remembrance versus merely audible devotion an explicit worship test.

column5: Jesus invokes the house of prayer while cleansing the temple
column6: Jesus calls the temple a house of prayer for all nations while driving out sellers; this reception of Isaiah 56:7 makes the worship place's name and purpose a critique of corrupted practice.

column5: Jesus says he made the Father's name known
column6: In a prayer for his disciples, Jesus says he revealed the Father's name to them and that they kept his word; this joins the commentary's remembered name to reception and faithful action.

column5: The name made known so love may dwell in disciples
column6: Jesus says he has made the Father's name known and will continue doing so, so divine love may be in the disciples; the prayer gives remembrance a continuing communal result.

column5: Every word and deed done in the Lord's name
column6: Paul tells the community to do every word and deed in Jesus' name, giving thanks to the Father; this closely joins voiced remembrance, bodily action, and gratitude.

column5: Prayer with lifted holy hands and clean relations
column6: Paul wants men to pray everywhere, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute; this is a specific embodied prayer whose moral posture matters.

column5: Draw near with cleansed hearts and washed bodies
column6: The community is invited to draw near with sincere hearts, hearts cleansed from an evil conscience, and bodies washed; this closely joins purification to embodied approach in prayer.

column5: Psalms and songs voiced from the heart
column6: The community is told to address one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing from the heart; this connects audible and inward praise as in the commentary's account of remembrance.

column5: Thanksgiving to God in Jesus' name
column6: The next verse commands continual thanks to God the Father in Jesus' name, explicitly binding remembrance of the name to prayerful gratitude.

column5: A community devoted to prayers and shared worship
column6: The first believers persist in teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers; this gives a communal form to the commentary's individual portrait without making prayer an isolated act.

column5: The Most High is not contained in handmade houses
column6: Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands; this qualifies the commentary's extension from one person's prayer to named worship buildings by placing God's presence beyond their walls.

column5: Worship is not confined to a sacred location
column6: Jesus says true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth, not by privileging either Jerusalem or the mountain; this offers a distinct Christian reading alongside the commentary's temple-and-prayer-place image.

column5: A people formed as a spiritual house and priesthood
column6: Believers are built into a spiritual house to offer spiritual sacrifices; this recasts the commentary's many worship houses as a worshipping community.

column5: The Father's name marks the worshippers
column6: The Lamb's followers have the Lamb's and Father's name written on their foreheads; this concretely meets the commentary's secondary image of a name as an identifying mark, without implying that the ayah uses that etymology.

column5: The redeemed sing a new song before the throne
column6: The marked group sings a song that only the redeemed can learn; this gives voiced praise as a communal consequence of bearing the name.

column5: Abram's prayer contrasts the Creator with idols
column6: The passage continues Abram's prayer against the worship of created things; the connection to the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's unique name is specific but depends on the remembered continuation of Jubilees' wording.

column5: The runner's race as disciplined religious effort
column6: The commentary records a secondary Arabic use of ṣallā for a horse immediately following the leader; Paul uses a footrace to describe striving for an imperishable prize, a plausible race image parallel that does not define the ayah's prayer verb.

column5: The body disciplined in the race
column6: Paul says he disciplines his body and makes it his servant; this is a limited counterpart to the commentary's bodily and race-following secondary imagery, not a claim that prayer means athletic training.
